articles.title: Strings Attached: The House Hearing on Renewing USPTO Fee Setting Authority
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
The House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, Artificial Intelligence, and the Internet held its hearing on renewal of USPTO fee setting authority on September 2, 2026, one day after the House passed the continuing resolution that extends the authority through December 11. Chairman Darrell Issa opened with his view that the question for December is not whether to renew but on what terms. That is the same advice that I gave House staffers when I discussed the issues with them last month.
Four witnesses testified, and none argued against renewal. Former Director David Kappos (who pushed through the original fee structure in 2011) asked for a clean seven- or eight-year extension with no policy riders. The other three wanted strings. Former Acting Director Teresa Stanek Rea proposed a two-year reauthorization cycle plus new statutory guardrails, including a requirement that the Office issue written reasons for PTAB institution decisions. Morgan Reed of the Association for Competitive Technology asked for a real sunset, a functioning PPAC, and limits on discretionary denial. Professor Melissa Wasserman of Texas Law recommended three to four years, structured financial reporting, and a GAO study.
Wasserman is a particularly apt witness for this issue. She, along with Professor Michael Frakes, has published a series of articles building an empirical case that the Office's fee structure shapes its granting decisions. But the 2024 Fee Study commissioned by the USPTO dismissed her work without ever truly engaging.
I wrote about the fee extension issues in a prior August 2026 post, laying out the leverage issue: IPR discretionary denial has nothing to do with fees, but the fee sunset is the one moment when the Office must come to Congress and ask for something.

articles.title: An Ordinary Word: T-Mobile v. KAIFI and What Counts as a Patent Case
articles.content:
丹尼斯·克劳奇撰文
我在2026年5月曾撰文介绍T-Mobile与KAIFI案，当时法庭辩论主要集中在一个关键问题上：联邦巡回法院是否对本案拥有上诉管辖权？如今答案已明朗——法院并无管辖权。陈法官与特兰托、施尔法官一致裁定，德州违约判决中包含的“专利权利要求是否经得起局外重审”的判定并不涉及专利法。法院同时出具一份非权威性的指令，将上诉案移送第五巡回法院。

该案涉及一份和解协议。KAIFI曾就其Wi-Fi呼叫专利（美国专利号6,922,728）起诉T-Mobile。双方在开庭前数日达成和解，T-Mobile获授许可、支付首期款并承诺若“任何被指控权利要求经得起EPR（局外重审）”，则支付第二期款。专利局后确认八项被指控权利要求中的七项无需修改。T-Mobile拒付款项，向吉尔斯特拉普法官提起多样性宣告判决诉讼，但以未能通过简易判决告败。吉尔斯特拉普法官裁定合约条款明确：若重审证书确认该权利要求，则视为“经得起”重审。双方均请联邦巡回法院裁定上诉，但法院拒绝，认为其缺乏上诉管辖权，并（有点奇怪地）花了数页解释其对合约条款的理解。
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

I wrote about T-Mobile v. KAIFI back in May 2026 following oral arguments where the court spent most of the time on one question: does the Federal Circuit have jurisdiction over this appeal?

The answer, we now know, is no.  Judge Chen, joined by Judges Taranto and Schall, held that a Texas breach of contract judgment that included a judgment on whether patent claims "survive" an ex parte reexamination does not arise under the patent laws. A companion nonprecedential order transfers the appeal to the Fifth Circuit.

The contract at issue was a settlement agreement. KAIFI had sued T-Mobile on its Wi-Fi calling U.S. Patent No. 6,922,728.  The parties settled days before trial, with T-Mobile taking a license, making an upfront payment, and promising a second payment if "any Asserted Claim survives the EPR" that T-Mobile itself had requested. The Patent Office then confirmed seven of the eight asserted claims without amendment. T-Mobile refused to pay, filed a diversity declaratory judgment action, and lost on summary judgment before Judge Gilstrap, who held the term unambiguous: a claim survives if the reexamination certificate confirms it. Both parties asked the Federal Circuit to decide the appeal. The panel declined, finding it lacked appellate jurisdiction, and then (oddly?) spent several pages explaining what it thinks the contract means.
